title: UK government investment arm cops to 40-hour leak of officials' contact details
teaser: A major security breach at UK Government Investments left a file with 51 officials' private contact details open to the public for 40 hours.
summary: UK Government Investments (UKGI), the Treasury-owned body advising on major government deals, admitted to a significant data leak. An employee failed to adhere to security policy, leaving an internal document with names and work email addresses of 51 officials publicly accessible for roughly 40 hours. UKGI voluntarily disclosed this breach to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), even though it wasn't mandatory. While an external review concluded that UKGI’s response was appropriate and recommended improving security controls, the report lacks detail on when or how the data was accessed. The leak raises concerns about governmental information security protocols amidst UKGI's involvement in major commercial deals like offloading NatWest shares.
content: SECURITY UK government investment arm cops to 40-hour leak of officials' contact details Employee failed to follow security policy, leaving internal management file open to the public The UK government's corporate finance adviser has admitted that an employee left an internal file containing the names and work email addresses of dozens of officials publicly accessible for around 40 hours. The breach, first reported by The Guardian , was disclosed in UK Government Investments' (UKGI) annual report , which says it occurred during the 2025-26 financial year after a member of staff "did not follow established information security policies." The exposed document contained "high-level management information" alongside the names and work email addresses of 51 government officials. UKGI, the Treasury-owned outfit that advises ministers on everything from corporate rescues to billion-dollar share sales, said it voluntarily reported the incident to the UK's Information Commissioner's Office even though it did not meet the threshold for mandatory notification. It also informed its Audit and Risk Committee and commissioned an external review of the breach. The report offers little else in the way of detail. UKGI doesn't say when the exposure occurred, where the file was hosted, whether anyone accessed or downloaded it, or which departments employed the affected officials. It also doesn't identify the external firm that reviewed the incident or disclose the recommendations it made. The review concluded that UKGI's response was appropriate and recommended further improvements to its security controls and incident preparedness. According to the report, "the overwhelming majority" of those recommendations have either already been implemented or are due to be introduced in the coming months. The mishap comes in a year when UKGI had its fingerprints on some of Whitehall's biggest commercial deals, from finally offloading the government's remaining NatWest shares to advising on small modular reactor financing and supporting the Eutelsat capital raise and Royal Mail takeover. The Register has asked UKGI for further details, including what information the file contained beyond names and email addresses, where it was publicly accessible, whether there is any evidence it was accessed while exposed, and what additional safeguards have since been introduced. Whether this was merely embarrassing or exposed officials to a meaningful risk depends on details UKGI has yet to disclose. An ICO spokesperson said: "We can confirm UK Government Investments Ltd reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." ®

title: Google Earth's AI makeover survives one trip around the Sun
teaser: Google Earth's new AI feature, which lets users generate reality-warping images from text prompts over real satellite data, was quickly rolled back due to rampant misinformation risk.
summary: Google initially launched an AI image generation feature, dubbed 'Nano Banana,' within Google Earth, allowing users to create visualizations using natural language prompts over real satellite imagery. However, the tool's power proved a major liability; within days, it was paused because of the immediate threat of misuse for generating highly believable misinformation. While Google argues that every generated image includes a SynthID digital watermark for verification, experts warn that even sophisticated fakes—such as alterings images showing 'refugees near the Mexican border' or bomb craters—can spread easily.
content: AI AND ML Google Earth's AI makeover survives one trip around the Sun Turns out letting anyone rewrite the planet with a prompt had drawbacks Google performed a remarkably brisk reverse ferret last week, launching AI image generation in Google Earth and yanking it the next day after certain sections of the internet did the inevitable. This is how it began : "Today we're bringing AI image generation with Nano Banana to Google Earth, letting you virtually reimagine anywhere in the real world." This is how it's going , less than 48 hours later: "Thanks for your submissions, we appreciate it - unfortunately we have seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we've rolled back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails." Never mind "this is why we can't have nice things." What exactly did Google expect when it added AI image generation to Google Earth? The process was simple - zoom into anywhere on Google Earth, hit "Create Image," enter a prompt to twist satellite imagery to reflect your hopes and dreams, then enjoy your creation. Or, as users quickly demonstrated, misinformation. While Google included cutesy examples of animal resorts, construction renderings, and restorations of ancient ruins, the darker side of the internet soon showed itself. AI tools have long been able to alter screenshots, but placing the generator inside a service trusted as a record of the physical world does no favors for that trust, despite Google's insistence that the output was watermarked as AI-generated. In an update, Google stated: "We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world," which makes the functionality even more bizarre. As AI and misinformation expert Henk van Ess noted in his Digital Digging blog, "What on earth is Google doing?" The AI misinformation genie has long left its bottle when it comes to imagery. However, putting a photorealistic image generator inside Google Earth and expecting only harmless fun shows Microsoft Tay levels of naivete. In retrospect, Tay, the AI chatbot that netizens persuaded to spew some impressively hateful tweets, offered a warning back in 2016 of what was coming down the line. Google has not permanently pulled the plug. As van Ess noted : "The feature is paused, not cancelled." ®

title: NASA boss balks at billion-dollar estimate for recycled Moon rover
teaser: NASA's boss balked at multi-billion dollar estimates for Moon rover built from repurposed Mars parts.
summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman criticized the high cost estimates for PROMISE, a proposed lunar rover mission that aims to leverage existing Mars rover testbeds (OPTIMISM and MAGGIE) from Perseverance and Curiosity. The Planetary Society estimated the total cost could reach $1.33 billion. However, Isaacman rejected even minor increases in expenditure, arguing that adapting these hardware models for lunar conditions might be prohibitively difficult and costly. He concluded that repurposing the testbeds could be more expensive than developing a dedicated system.
content: SCIENCE NASA boss balks at billion-dollar estimate for recycled Moon rover Turning two Mars testbeds into one lunar explorer may prove anything but cheap NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has stated "we simply will not fly it" if claims about the costs of the repurposed Mars rover engineering model prove anywhere near accurate. Isaacman was responding to the Planetary Society's chief of space policy, Casey Dreier, who had run the numbers on his plan to send a robot to the Moon, built from parts of engineering models of the successful Mars rovers Perseverance and Curiosity. Dreier estimated that the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration (PROMISE) mission, as discussed by Isaacman in a June presentation , would cost between $723 million and $1.33 billion. Dreier's figures include a low-end launch and landing cost of $234 million and a high-end estimate of $320 million. PROMISE is intended to put a rover on the Moon for a fraction of the usual cost. There are engineering testbeds for both Perseverance and Curiosity, dubbed OPTIMISM (Operational Perseverance Twin for Integration of Mechanisms and Instruments Sent to Mars) and MAGGIE (Mars Automated Giant Gizmo for Integrated Engineering) respectively. While not 100 percent identical to what was sent to Mars, the pair are designed to be close enough to allow engineers to perform activities such as plotting drives on simulated Martian terrain and seeing how the hardware will react to commands sent from Earth. NASA bosses looked at the engineering models, considered ways to score easy "wins," as Isaacman put it , and came up with an idea. Engineering models are common enough in spaceflight. A Development Test Model (DTM) of Voyager can be found hanging in the Exploring the Planets gallery at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC . The DTM's bus was liberated in 1987 for developing NASA's Magellan Venus spacecraft. The Register also paid a visit to a test model of the European Space Agency's Solar Orbiter on a 2022 visit to the agency's Darmstadt site, which looked more like an explosion of wiring than a simulacrum of a spacecraft. MAGGIE and OPTIMISM are at least recognizable as engineering testbeds for Curiosity and Perseverance, but getting a hybrid using parts from both models into a state where it can do useful science on the Moon would be a challenge. As well as qualifying the components for launch and spaceflight, engineers would have to prepare hardware built for use on Earth to withstand lunar conditions. Power and communications would also need work: NASA has a "spare" plutonium radioisotope power system, but the rover would require substantial adaptation to use it. Then there are the consequences of taking engineering models away from active missions. "Regardless of whether one agrees with every estimate... one thing is clear: PROMISE is far from a 'freebie,'" Dreier stated. Isaacman did not challenge individual elements of Dreier's breakdown, although he excluded launch and landing because those costs "are a reality for any mission." Even so, he said, "if PROMISE costs even 20 percent of your low-end estimate, we simply will not fly it." "That said, it would be crazy not to take advantage of hardware taxpayers have already invested hundreds of millions of dollars in." That hardware has already been taken advantage of. It was designed to be a testbed and used for that purpose. Repurposing them for a one-off mission to the Moon could prove more troublesome and expensive than designing a rover that can be mass-produced. ®

title: Google is working on Plugins for Gemini Enterprise
teaser: Google is evolving Gemini Enterprise into an "output factory" with new plugins and App tiles that let users build interactive workflows from source material.
summary: Google is significantly enhancing Gemini for enterprises by adding Plugins and a dedicated Notifications area to move beyond simple chat toward complex, reusable workflows. 'Plugins' are expected to function as mini-apps or packaged tools, combining existing Skills (reusable actions) with Connectors (links to services like Workspace/M365) to automate multi-step processes across company data. Additionally, a new Notifications area will manage long-running tasks and background agent jobs. Separately, Gemini Notebook is introducing an 'App' artifact type, allowing users to generate fully interactive applications (e.g., dashboards, study aids) directly from source documents. These features are still in development, reflecting Google's strategy of creating a governed service for sophisticated corporate workflows.
author: Alexey Shabanov
content: Google appears to be preparing Plugins and a dedicated Notifications area for the Gemini Enterprise app, extending its push beyond chat toward reusable workplace workflows. Clues in an unfinished interface show a revised Connectors area split into three tabs: Connectors, Skills, and Plugins. The Plugins tab is currently empty, indicating that the feature is still under development. Its placement suggests that Plugins may act as mini-apps or packaged workflows, combining reusable Skills with one or more Connectors. This could let business teams run multi-step processes across company data and services without configuring every component from scratch. The structure also resembles how Claude separates connectors and skills, while allowing packaged tools to build on both. A separate Notifications area is also being prepared. It is expected to collect completed Gemini responses from scheduled tasks and conversations placed in a queue, giving users one place to return to work that finished in the background. This would be particularly useful for employees running research, reporting, or other jobs that take longer than a standard chat response. The work fits Google's broader strategy for Gemini Enterprise , which brings agents, company data, and workflow controls into one governed service. Google already describes Skills as reusable actions, Connectors as links to services including Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, and Inbox as a central hub for long-running agent activity. Plugins would add a packaged application layer on top of those pieces. Google has not publicly announced the Plugins section or provided a rollout date. The empty catalog and unfinished Notifications interface indicate that both are still in development, with availability, supported accounts, and the first plugin partners remaining unknown.

title: Police National Legal Database confirms data theft after dark web leak
teaser: Major government databases are compromised: Cybercriminals stole 135,000 police records and over 607,000 parent details from DfE.
summary: Multiple major institutions are reeling from significant data theft incidents. The Police National Legal Database (PNLD), used by police forces, confirmed its operational data was compromised in a breach linked to the 'ExfilSquad' group. This notorious cyber-extortion outfit also targeted the Department for Education (DfE), exposing over 607,000 private records. Specific details confirm that ExfilSquad claimed 135,000 law enforcement contact records were stolen from PNLD. Furthermore, Advanced Procurement for Universities and Colleges (APUC) reported a separate intrusion involving historical data. These attacks highlight the vulnerability of critical public sector infrastructure to sophisticated cybercrime.
content: cyber-crime Police National Legal Database confirms data theft after dark web leak ExfilSquad claims 135,000 contact records weeks after hitting the Department for Education The Police National Legal Database (PNLD) is the latest UK public sector outfit to admit that cybercriminals made off with its data, including the names and work email addresses of police officers, justice staff, government partners, and customers. The legal lookup service relied upon by police forces and criminal justice agencies across the UK said it discovered the "data security incident" on July 26 and is investigating alongside specialist cybersecurity firms and the National Crime Agency. According to the PNLD, the leaked information includes the names, organizations, and work email addresses of police officers, police staff, criminal justice professionals, government partners, and customers. It insists there is "no evidence" that passwords or other authentication data were compromised. The breach also affected Ask the Police, a public-facing legal advice website operated by PNLD. There, the fallout appears limited to the names and email addresses of people who previously submitted questions through the service. That's about where the explanation ends. PNLD has yet to say how attackers got in, when the data was stolen, how many people were affected, or whether anyone tried to shake it down before the information appeared online. West Yorkshire Police, which operates PNLD, did not immediately respond to The Register's questions. However, the breach appears linked to the same extortion crew that last week claimed responsibility for a similar breach of the Department for Education (DfE). The group, which calls itself "ExfilSquad," currently lists both the PNLD and DfE among its latest victims on its dark web leak site, seen by The Register . For PNLD, the crooks claim to have lifted a 1.9 GB dataset containing roughly 135,000 law enforcement contact records, including names, email addresses, and police force areas. The DfE listing boasts of around 600,000 parent and staff contact records, plus another 7,000 from its Turing Portal. The education department confirmed last week that more than 607,000 records had indeed been exposed. The DfE has confirmed that the compromised information was limited to customer service contact details from its Customer Help Portal and Turing Scheme, and said no other departmental data had been accessed. Like most cyber-extortion outfits, ExfilSquad doesn't exactly do understatement. Its leak site warns victims that once data appears there, it is "NEVER leaving the public eye," before suggesting any ransom would amount to little more than a rounding error compared with the legal bills that might follow. The DfE and PNLD's confirmations don't validate everything ExfilSquad posts on its leak site. It also lists Microsoft as a victim, alleging a 13 GB haul containing millions of records, password hashes, internal support tickets, and access permissions. Having two organizations confirm breaches claimed on its leak site makes ExfilSquad harder to ignore. Whether the gang's other boasts are equally well founded, or simply the usual cybercrook embellishment, remains to be seen. ® Updated to add at 1517 UTC, August 3: The North East Regional Organised Crime Unit told The Reg it is investigating the breach. It told us "No ransom demand has been received." It also confirmed some numbers, stating the data of around 114,000 PNLD subscriber was involved. It added: "This involves the names, work email addresses and work organisation of police officers and other criminal justice partners. There are also around 21,000 email addresses of members of the public who have previously used 'Ask the Police'. There is no evidence to suggest that passwords or other security credentials have been compromised."

title: Spider-Man and The Odyssey are splitting up IMAX screens after a record-breaking weekend
teaser: Mega hits! After leading to a record $430M weekend, Spider-Man and The Odyssey are now splitting IMAX screens on August 6th.
summary: Box offices are buzzing following a record-breaking weekend, with 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' and Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' contributing to a massive $430 million total. Due to its monumental success, IMAX announced that *Spider-Man* will now share screens in select digital IMAX locations starting August 6th, as The Odyssey’s exclusive run ends. *Spider-Man: Brand New Day* achieved a strong debut of $355 million in North America. Meanwhile, 'The Odyssey' continues its global showing and has already grossed $221 million at the global IMAX box office.
author: Emma Roth
content: Spider-Man: Brand New Day is joining The Odyssey in IMAX theaters after both movies led the biggest weekend in box office history. On Monday, IMAX announced that Spider-Man: Brand New Day will be available in select digital IMAX locations across North America starting Thursday, August 6th. The news comes as The Odyssey 's exclusive three-weekend run in IMAX theaters comes to an end, allowing Spider-Man: Brand New Day to play alongside it, as reported by Variety . Spider-Man: Brand New Day raked in $355 million following its July 31st release, making it the second-biggest box office debut in North America since Avengers: Endgame in 2019. Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey had a similarly big weekend, pulling in $51 million weeks after its premiere. Both films - in addition to Toy Story 5 , Moana , Minions & Monsters - led to a record-breaking $430 million weekend at the box office, according to Variety . The Odyssey will continue playing in theaters across the global IMAX network. The film has already generated $221 million at the global IMAX box office, helping to make July IMAX's highest-grossing month in history . IMAX says The Odyssey is the only film that has driven "multiple $40 million-plus weekends" in its global box office.

title: Palworld’s expanding to mobile with a new MMORPG
teaser: Palworld is going mobile! Get ready to explore the open world of 'Palworld Online,' an MMORPG coming to iOS and Android this year.
summary:
Following its successful 1.0 launch, Palworld is expanding to mobile platforms (iOS and Android) with 'Palworld Online,' an open-world MMORPG developed by Garena. This new installment aims to maintain the depth of creature collecting while optimizing gameplay for touch screens. Players can look forward to familiar core features—including crafting and multiplayer modes (co-op, PvP, and PvE)—alongside a completely new narrative setting with exclusive story elements.

The game promises a streamlined interface, featuring optional one-tap controls suitable for base management on various mobile devices.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: After its 1.0 launch last month , Palworld is coming to iOS and Android with a new open-world MMORPG launching later this year, Polygon reports. Garena, the developer behind the new game, says in its announcement that Palworld Online "reimagines the depth, freedom, and scale of the original PC survival creature-collecting title for mobile." The core features of the new mobile game sound a lot like the original Palworld , with crafting, creature collecting, and multiplayer options for co-op, PvP, and PvE. Garena says it will introduce a "new narrative setting with original story elements," and "expand the narrative with new side stories created exclusively for this version." It will also have a "streamlined, touch-friendly interface with optional one-tap controls" to handle base management on different sized mobile screens. Palworld Online doesn't have a specific release date yet, but if it does come out this year, it could arrive before the Palfarm spin-off Pocketpair announced last year, which also doesn't have a release date yet.

title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
teaser: Bluesky's new CEO frames the open protocol AT Protocol and the associated 'ATmosphere' as the necessary future standard for social media, echoing early web principles.
summary: The interview details Toni Schneider's vision for Bluesky, which operates on two levels: the user-facing app and the underlying, open AT Protocol. This protocol allows over a thousand interoperable applications to thrive in what Schneider calls the 'ATmosphere,' establishing the future of social media centered on public good, rather than proprietary algorithms or ads. Building on his experience at Automattic (WordPress), Schneider emphasizes that moving from interim to full-time CEO signals commitment and stability to the development community. He compares the current period to the early days of the web, arguing for a return to an open ecosystem model amidst fragmented modern platforms.
author: Nilay Patel
content: Today, I'm talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky - he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky's prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show - she's now the company's chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all. Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There's a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there's the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you'll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing - it's called the ATmosphere, which is adorable. But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team. Verge subscribers, don't forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you'll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop. That's quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky's reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue - and interestingly enough, it's not just ads. This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you're gonna like it. Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of BlueSky. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. Thanks for having me. I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there's something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. Do you want BlueSky to get there where it's just one player among many, or do you want to retain control of the standard too? And how do you think that's different from how Automattic exists in the web ecosystem? We 100% do not want to control the standard at BlueSky. We are actually very actively doing everything in our power to divest control of it. First was to design the network in a way that if BlueSky goes down or goes away, the rest of the network is fine. That's a big test case for us. It actually got tested a couple of months ago, not the way we had hoped, but we got a DDoS attack on the BlueSky network. A very, very massive one. It did take us down for several hours. Other parts of the network, like I mentioned BlackSky earlier, operated just fine, totally independently. That's a big part. Just the practicality of it is, can other nodes in this network operate independently? Are there things left that BlueSky runs that everybody else is dependent on? And if so, what can we do to fix that? A big part of that, too, is that - this gets a little nerdy into the whole stack and the protocol - when people look at the design of this network and they like to find out, is it truly decentralized or not? There is one thing at the heart of it that absolutely no company should control, and that's the identity directory, the lookup. When you log in your identity in the ATmosphere, where does that lookup actually happen? It's like DNS on the web when somebody looks up a URL. We have been running that core directory, and we're actually in the process of setting up a Swiss nonprofit with a separate board, a completely separate entity, to which we've handed over that directory. We're in the process of handing over the domain to it. So that's one example. We're also handing the protocol spec itself to the IETF. Last week, the IETF met in Vienna, and AT Proto is now a work stream, an official work stream to take that out of BlueSky and hand it to the IETF. It's going to become a blessed internet standard run by a completely separate entity. We're constantly taking all the pieces that we had to bootstrap and handing them off to other entities. We're super serious about that. The end state is that, yes, we are one app of many, one company of many running in this protocol, and we won't control the protocol. The parallel to Automattic is that WordPress, the core software that Automattic is hosting, is open source and it's GPL. Anybody can use it, but anybody who uses it and changes it has to give back to open source. In our case, it's AT Protocol where anybody can build on AT Protocol. The beauty of building on AT Proto as a developer is all the data is owned by users and it's accessible to any other app. But as an app, then your data also goes into those user repositories. So it makes it better for everybody else on the network. It's similar to the way open source gets better through collaboration. This network gets better through everybody having their data shared and remixable and interoperable. When you get that balance right - or you have a company that helps bootstrap the whole thing, but by definition keeps itself separate and makes sure it can't control the shared resource - then it can work. We did this successfully with Automattic and WordPress. Automattic became a big company. WordPress became a huge open source ecosystem, and then tons of other companies formed around it. Our test case was always, "What if Automattic goes out of business or gets acquired by somebody evil? Is WordPress going to be okay?" That's why we put the WordPress trademark into a foundation so the company couldn't mess with it. It's complicated to set those things up. This is one of those, not even five years, like 20 years out decisions. If this thing gets big, will it be truly independent? Or could somebody come in and change their mind and mess with it? We think about that constantly at BlueSky and getting that balance right. Handing off pieces so that this - because it's not going to work if one company tries to control it, we're right back at square one and we're just another walled garden, which is completely the opposite of what we're trying to achieve. There's a lot of drama with WordPress and the open-source community and other companies monetizing open-source in different ways. There's drama with the foundation . I'll set that all aside. People can go listen to Matt's episodes . We did it in detail, and certainly will have him back. I like talking to Matt a lot. But that's all coming for you too, because at some point all of this has to make money. A real theme on Decoder is we've set up complicated structures so that capitalism can't ruin everything. We just had Proton on the show . Complicated Swiss foundation structure so that capitalism can't ruin everything and all the promises they make to their customers. You don't have that problem yet. As far as I can tell, there's no revenue flowing into this and probably thus no push to make that revenue number go up in bad ways. At some point there is going to have to be some revenue. You're an investor. I'm assuming you want to get paid out into your own fund. How is BlueSky going to make money on the app level, and how is the protocol going to make any money? The way we're going to make money as a company, we're only interested if that economic model works for the entire ATmosphere. We make money when everybody else makes money. That rules out a bunch of things that will be purely app-based. I'm not ready to announce the specifics, but we will start monetizing this year. The way I look at it is there's already money being made on this network. We're sending lots of traffic to people who then convert that traffic into subscriptions.. I think our job is to just help more of that happen. Right now it's just organic, and we can build things into our app and into the protocol that make it easier for people to start making a livelihood on this protocol and start doing ecommerce with each other. That's the direction we're headed in. We're going to do it in a way where the whole idea is for the pie to get huge and for us to be a small slice of a big pie and for everybody to make money. If we can help you as a publisher make more money, then we can do business together. I know you said you weren't going to do specifics, but I have to poke at this a little bit. Your options, if you want a small piece of a big pie, are "We're going to let you run ads for your subscription newsletter and then that'll convert." That's Facebook's model, right? "We're going to let you run ads at whatever CPM, and your return on ad spend will be high enough so that enough subscribers signed up based on how many ads you were on." And the other one is, "We're just going to take a percentage of every signup fee." Which direction do you think you're headed in? It would definitely be the latter, but we would only take a percentage of anything that we actually enable. If we send extra traffic to you, then it would be a percentage of that. So basically affiliate-style monetization. If I'm selling a newsletter for $10 a month and you send me a new subscriber, you're going to get some of that back. Affiliate style and in a way that works for the entire network. Anybody on the network that sends you traffic can participate. We want everybody to have a part in it. Can you decentralize the billing and financial layer of that? We can make it work in a decentralized network. Billing does require some centralized trust, and that's certainly something we're looking at. I asked you that question because I was terrified of a crypto scheme basically, but it does not sound like you're going to do crypto schemes. No, no. Similar intentions, but definitely not a crypto approach. One of the things that you've been describing is, "We have to build all these structures to withstand the bad incentives. If somebody shows up and buys BlueSky, and they've got bad intentions or they just want to use it to do crypto schemes, we have to build the structure that will withstand it." Adding monetization in whatever form - and I agree the network should be monetized in some way - creates a bunch of these incentives at first launch. It will be your first contact with those incentives. You have some experience with this, certainly even thinking about it. How do you expect that to go both with your team and with the user base of BlueSky itself? The team is eager to figure this out because we realize that there has to be an economic model for this network. Otherwise, we're in the early bootstrap phase still and lots of people are getting excited to build on this. But it's the number-one question for my team, from all the people building. "What's that model going to be?" Everybody's eager to figure this out and to do it in a way that we don't fall into the traps of trying to create the incentives that we've seen in other networks, which just cause all kinds of unintended consequences. Looping back on the WordPress example, it can work really nicely. WordPress is a slightly different model because it's a hosting model. But there are thousands and thousands of WordPress hosts out there that are doing just fine and it just works. You can host your site anywhere, you can move it anywhere. They compete to be the best host for your content, but it's a very good model. As far as I can tell, it hasn't created anybody to take all the market share or create these weird incentives where the product gets worse. There's a very nice dividing line there between "I'm your host" and "you go and do whatever you want." You can build an ad network if you want. You can build a store, you can build something else. Our business model doesn't dictate what your business model should be, which is kind of what happens in these other networks when it's only ads. "Oh yeah, come here, build your following on here and then we're going to put ads on it. If you want to do anything else, no, no, no, it's going to be ads." Those are the kinds of things we think about. Talking about irreversible decisions, that's going to be a huge one when we start to zero in on the right model to make sure that we can picture this scaling to billions of users and all kinds of businesses emerging on this network, not just one type that we happen to think about. You've mentioned BlackSky a handful of times in this conversation. I've been lucky enough to be at a dinner with Rudy [Fraser] who runs BlackSky. He's prolific in talking about what it's like to actually build on the ATmosphere and what a lot of the challenges have been. Because it hasn't yet really, truly been decentralized. Now it's my turn to say, I won't go into the weeds of the protocol, but there are parts of the BlueSky stack and parts of the ATmosphere that have been pretty heavily centralized up until fairly recently. Is it easy to stand up a competitor, in the way that you're describing people can stand up competitors to WordPress and operate in their own universe using the same tools and same access to end customers? Or is there still work to be done there? Because it hasn't been easy up until now, at least using the example of BlackSky. Rudy deserves a lot of credit for taking those early risks when it was much harder to build and being the first to prove that it can be done, but it's getting easier and easier. We are seeing more and more BlueSky- and BlackSky-style networks pop up pretty often. We're actually seeing a whole bunch of energy in Europe. We've got EuroSky. W Social just launched. There's another one I think that's about to launch. It's getting easier, and we're investing a lot to make it as easy as possible. In addition to being an open protocol, all of BlueSky's open source. You can take the BlueSky app and just fork it and go do your own BlueSky. That's great, but we're really also interested in people building other things that are microblogging on the network and making that super easy. We're seeing Tangled as an example that a lot of people like to use recently because it's a great project. They raised VC funding. It's a social coding platform, like a social GitHub that's growing really nicely using AT Proto for the social layer of the social coding aspect. Has nothing to do with microblogging, but it's another thing that we can collaborate and integrate. People use both Tangled and BlueSky. It all just works together. But those are examples where it's getting really easy to just build a new app on AT Proto and have it have social functionality. It doesn't have to be an entire BlueSky-style network that you have to run. We put effort into making it easier. When BlackSky started two or three years ago, it was a big lift. You had to be very technical to do it. Now it's gotten easier and easier. Finally, we haven't talked about AI yet. AI makes it even easier. A lot of the growth we're seeing now is that you can point to one of the AI coding tools on AT Proto and say, "Hey, build me a social app, build me a community." And that makes it that much easier. Those are some of the tools and integrations that we're working on on Jay's new team, but that really changes the game pretty substantially for just how easy all this stuff is getting. I do have to ask you the AI question. You're a software CEO again. How do software companies work in the age of AI? Have you rethought your teams? Do you have the traditional product-manager-designer-engineer trio? Or is everybody doing everything? It's a small team and you're the new CEO. So you have lots of opportunity to rethink everything. It is very empowering once you get it right. We have to use our exploration team as an example. That's a three- to four-person team that's launching at very high velocity, launching brand new products. It's really fun when you have an existing company with existing resources and very senior talented people can then go after a new greenfield opportunity with these new tools. That's when you see a ton of velocity. If you have an existing product with all the complexity of how it's been built, AI helps, but you're still dealing with that same complexity for a while. I see it accelerate everything in terms of the development pace. You still need great product managers, you need great designers. You need [to know] how to build. The building part is faster than what to build. The ideas are just as hard as ever, in a way harder because there's so much noise out there and so many things popping up every day. Setting yourself apart, building something really great that lasts. Just because it's faster with AI doesn't make it any easier. We've talked a lot about standards and making AT Protocol and the ATmosphere a more standardized project at the IETF and whatever Swiss foundation is going to do name lookups. It feels like we're going to recapitulate ICANN. But that's a totally different episode of Decoder , and we'll come to that drama when everything is successful. There is another standard that has already gone through all this. There's ActivityPub. Mastodon runs an ActivityPub. Famously, Threads runs an ActivityPub, to whatever extent Threads runs on ActivityPub. There's an argument that Meta did all of that just to satisfy European regulators, and that's all it's there for. Have you talked to the Threads team about integrating with ActivityPub or moving them to the ATmosphere? Once you become an official standard, I imagine that must be easier for them to continue throwing bones to European regulators. That would be the big unlock, right? That is the hundreds of millions of users on a nominally open network. Have they shown any interest? We have not talked to Threads. We're definitely talking to Mastodon and ActivityPub. They definitely feel we're very aligned. Our missions are very aligned. We're all on Team Open together. These are two different standards that do slightly different things. And some use cases for ActivityPub are great and some are great for AT Proto. What are use cases that are good in ActivityPub and what are use cases that are better in AT Protocol? ActivityPub is based around this notion of a server. At the heart of it, you set up your own server, you control it, you run it, that's your community, and then all the servers can federate if you want. You don't have to, you can just run it by yourself, or you can plug into the federation, into the Fediverse. That's how their system works. It works really well. They have a lot of successful governments who want to set up their own server infrastructure and run their own community infrastructure. AT Proto has a different goal. We don't have a server at the heart of it. We have the PDS, the personal data server that is your data. The heart of AT Proto is personal identity and portability and ownership of that so that whatever you create and the social graph that you create is owned by you and lifts wherever you want to host it. It's really a federation of millions and millions of these tiny little personal servers that can all talk to each other. That works if your social product is focused on people, not on an entire server with a community on it. So a slightly different shape. They interoperate too. There's something called Bridgy Fed that connects these two worlds together. So if you've built products on this yourself, if you want to post or publish across all of it, you can and the end user doesn't even have to know. That's the beauty of an open protocol: you shouldn't have to. Consumers of this should never even hear about these new protocols. Because it's one of these things where you have to get the protocol right and it has to be open, but then people should just forget about it. It should just disappear. The examples we use a lot are email and websites. If I'm on Outlook and you're on Gmail, we can just email each other. You never think about the fact that those are two completely separate systems. It just works. But on social media, it just doesn't work that way. If you're on Instagram and I'm on TikTok, we can't talk to each other. You have to do everything five different times and on five different apps, and it's crazy making. If we get this right at the protocol level, that just goes away. All this stuff just works just like email does or just like websites do. Our job is to make all of that work under the hood, but nobody has to think about it. In the end, you just have one account, you log in anywhere and it just works, and all your friends are there and all your data's there. And you never have to be locked in again into somebody's system [where] you can't leave. This is very nice, but it's rare that two standards that nominally seek to achieve the same thing coexist forever. There are not two Bluetooths, there are not two Wi-Fis. There are not even two webs. People can argue with me about how many webs there are, but there are not even two webs. Do you expect ActivityPub and AT Protocol to coexist? Do you expect, I don't know, BlueSky to be able to show content from Mastodon servers and then slowly eat ActivityPub as a protocol? That's one very common pattern that happens in these situations. Or do you expect long-term coexistence? I expect long-term coexistence because both of these protocols have enough users and use cases that want to continue on. They can talk to each other when you want, but that's not the main use of it. There are a lot of people who run ActivityPub instances who don't even want to talk to other Mastodon servers. They just want to run their own thing. They don't want to talk to AT Proto, but they can if they want. I don't know what a good example is from other platforms. But they're both going to be around for a long time and they're just slightly different tools. They're both in the social space, but they're different tools that you reach to for different types of use cases. I'll put it this way: In my mind, both can be wildly successful, and it's not one or the other. AT Proto doesn't need to eat ActivityPub to be successful, or vice versa. We've already seen that. I want to end by talking about the consumer app a little bit more. We've talked a lot about the protocol, the ATmosphere, the standards. We've gotten all the way to the internet engineering task force in this conversation. We've been in the weeds of how the technology works and how it's governed. And right next to that is, well, it's an election year here in the United States. And a lot of people truly believe that BlueSky is the wild progressive social media network and it is a bubble of one kind. X is a very different kind of bubble. It's the hard-right network that has vastly more AI-generated anime porn on it. There's not some thing that is actually the global town square. That thing has maybe gone away and all the social networks have fragmented. Do you want BlueSky to have the reputation it has? Do you want it to get bigger? Do you think that the right answer is someone starts a MAGA BlueSky and it interoperates the way that it needs to? This is the perception of the consumer product. Do you want that to change, and how would you change it? Yes, we definitely want that to change. It is already changing. It certainly wasn't designed to attract one specific group of people. It works for anyone. What we see is there is a lot of political discourse on BlueSky and any of these open networks. People are very engaged. What we've seen in the lead up to the election so far - we've hosted a lot of live election feeds, and we see a lot of really good feedback from our users, a lot of engagement, a lot of, "This is actually really interesting content about this topic." Whereas on other platforms, I think these election topics just get completely overwhelmed by slop and spam. It's just noise and chaos. What we're focusing on is to deliver a live experience. We do it around elections. We do it around sports as well, very successfully, where the people on the network that participate get a really good experience and get really good content. Once we have that, then hopefully we can just keep expanding to more and more types of users and use cases. We're an open network for anyone and we don't want to serve just one type of user base. I've seen it already in the last few months, really trend in the right direction where we just have more and more people show up and build their own corners of the network. It sort of balances out over time. We don't just have a few topics you're super deep on, but it just gets more and more diverse. In my opinion, yes, it's a public square, but we don't need everybody talking at the same time. Policy is very loaded, but if you're super into sports, you're not going to be into all sports. I'm super into the San Francisco Giants, so that's what I want to follow. I don't need to follow all of sports, and that's fine. It can be like that with all topics. It just needs to be civil and positive and we need to have the tools that if it goes off the rails, people can regulate it and can have a good experience instead of it just devolving into a shouting match. By "people can regulate it," you mean people can moderate their own feeds, not regulators can moderate speech? Just checking. That's important. Build their own feeds, pick their own feeds. We have very good tools for people to mute and block. We spend a lot of energy on making sure it stays positive because again, we're interested in social media that actually serves the common or the public good. That's not going to work if it's just people yelling. You've talked a lot about the network. Even in this answer, I said BlueSky the app has this reputation, and you started talking about the network. It's true, the network can serve everybody. Anybody can start whatever kind of app on the ATmosphere they want and they can go target the users they want. But I want to push you again on BlueSky the app. The thing that has a brand that exists out in the world that is totally divorced from the technical specifications of the ATmosphere. There is BlueSky the app and it does have a reputation. Do you want more users from X to leave X and join BlueSky and expand what that brand is for people? Yes. It can stay on X too. You don't have to pick one or the other, but yes. Have you talked to Elon about federating X? I suspect he's not interested. No, same answer with Threads. It would be full circle, right? BlueSky started inside Twitter, and then Twitter went away and became X. And then if X adopted AT Proto, then the whole original idea of the project would actually come to fruition. Yeah. This is Jack Dorsey saying Twitter wants to be AT Protocol, not a product. Here we are, and that's BlueSky in big ways, but it is also a product. People know what that logo means. Political pundits say "the BlueSky crowd," and that signifies whatever they want it to signify. I'm just wondering if you want to break that branding in any meaningful way. Yeah, we want to expand it. "Breaking" is maybe the wrong word, but yes, we want to expand more and more so that BlueSky means not just one thing, not just liberal politics, for example. I will point to sports as an example from the last year. We've made a very concerted effort to bring on sports leagues and sports writers, and it's worked really well. There are a ton of sports conversations now on the app, and those people come here for the sports, not for the liberal politics. It's possible to expand. In politics, it's probably our hardest challenge because we have one type of user base there that's very active. That's good too. They are super active, and they're very much at the forefront of politics and very engaged and very informed. But we can just keep adding more communities so that it balances out. It feels like we're going to have to have you back, particularly as these private communities launch, to talk about where things go from here. But this has been great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thank you very much for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! title: Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a meeting notetaker, updated terms suggest
teaser: Dictation app Wispr Flow is expanding into the competitive market of meeting intelligence by launching a powerful notetaker feature, generating summaries and actions from audio inputs.
summary: Dictation app Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a sophisticated meeting notetaker, as revealed in updated Terms of Service. This new feature moves beyond simple dictation, allowing it to generate AI-powered transcripts, summaries, action items, and insights. The tool can process extensive 'Meeting Data,' including audio, participant information, and metadata. By adding this functionality, Wispr Flow aims to compete with established notetakers like Granola, Fireflies, Otter, and Fathom. Financed by over $81 million, the company's valuation was previously reported at $700 million.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: Dictation app Wispr Flow is preparing to launch a meeting notetaker, according to the tool's updated Terms of Service. The company also sent an email to its customers about the change in both its terms and its privacy policy to accommodate related features. Upon investigation, the refreshed terms have added sections about the use of meeting data and the notetaker. The company said the notetaker will generate transcripts, summaries, actions, and insights, writing: "For Notetaker, Input may also include Meeting Data, including meeting audio, participant information, meeting metadata, speaker labels, meeting transcripts, and other information processed in connection with a meeting. Output may include AI-generated meeting transcripts, summaries, action items, meeting insights, speaker attribution, and other meeting-related content." With the launch, the startup will take on other meeting notetakers such as Granola , Fireflies , Read AI , Otter , and Fathom . Wispr Flow's co-founder Tanay Kothari had previously talked about building an AI assistant in interviews . With a meeting notetaker, Wispr Flow would gain additional context about its users and could automate more tasks beyond cleaning up spoken sentences. It's not clear if the startup wants to launch a Granola-style notetaker that relies on system audio and transcribes the meeting without keeping a recording, or build a full-fledged meeting recording tool. To date, Wispr Flow has raised more than $81 million , with the company valued at $700 million at its last round. In May, Bloomberg reported that the company was in talks for a new round, valuing it at $2 billion. Wispr Flow didn't respond to our request for further comment.

title: Microsoft is bringing Xbox 360 games to PC
teaser: Microsoft plans to let developers bring Xbox 360 games to PC in a push toward console-free gaming, fundamentally changing how game libraries are distributed.
summary: Microsoft is expanding its Xbox ecosystem by planning to allow developers to port their Xbox 360 titles to PC. This move complements the planned launch of original Xbox games on PC and aims to build a cross-device library for future consoles (Project Helix) and handhelds. Developers can opt into backward compatibility, retaining control over pricing and Game Pass availability. The rollout is scheduled for a gradual release between 2027 and 2028. Separately, the 'disc-to-digital' program allows users to receive digital licenses for physical games sold on older consoles (Xbox One/Series), ensuring these licenses remain transferable even if the disc changes hands.
author: Tom Warren
content: Building on its recently announced plans to bring original Xbox games to PC , Microsoft is also planning to let developers bring their Xbox 360 games to PC as well, according to a leaked document, seen by The Verge , that was sent to developers recently. Xbox 360 games will be able to run on the next-gen Project Helix console, "Xbox PCs," and handheld devices, the document says. Microsoft has already said that Helix will play PC games , so making these older Xbox titles available on PC helps build a broader Xbox library that can travel between devices, similar to what's already possible with Steam. Creating all these digital licenses also helps set up for a future of consoles without disc drives; Sony has already declared game discs dead , and Microsoft may follow . With 360 games, developers can opt into making them backward compatible, and they will have control over things like a game's price and if it's available on Game Pass. The feature is expected to have a "gradual" rollout between 2027 and 2028 "across next-gen devices." The "full launch" of original Xbox games on PC is also set for October 2026; the initial program announced in July included just four games. The document also includes details about a way for players to get a digital version of a game that they already own on a physical disc, which The Verge 's Tom Warren reported on in July . The document says that if a player puts an Xbox One or Series game on disc into an Xbox One or Series X console with a disc drive, they'll be granted a digital license that's bound to "that disc and the player's account." The license will stay with a player across Xbox devices, but if the disc "changes hands," the license will transfer to the new person. That should mean that gamers can still trade and sell discs; once the original owner of a disc does so, they can't play the digital version they got from that disc anymore. According to the document, a public beta for the disc-to-digital program was set for July with general availability set for August. We understand Microsoft had originally planned to test its disc-to-digital program with Xbox Insiders in July, but the beta was delayed. It's unclear if the timeline of August general availability is still accurate. The planned changes follow Microsoft's major Xbox "reset" announced in July , which included thousands of layoffs and the company selling off four studios.

title: AI's next trade war: Robots
teaser: The U.S. may ban foreign robots despite its reliance on cheap Chinese tech: A policy conflict threatening AI innovation.
summary:
The debate around AI protectionism centers on whether the U.S. should restrict foreign-made robots, especially those from China. The administration is reportedly moving to protect domestic AI industries by considering bans on open-source Chinese models and humanoids, citing cybersecurity risks (like unauthorized control of vacuum cleaners). While this aligns with previous trade strategies to boost domestic tech, industry experts warn that the move could hamstring research.

US robotics labs rely heavily on cheap Chinese models because they offer a superior price-to-capability ratio. With Unitree's humanoids costing significantly less than comparable US models, an outright ban risks stunting crucial research and slowing down the rapidly emerging sector.
author: The Algorithm from MIT Technology Review
content: On its face, it's a strategy to align political and industry interests that is much older than the Trump administration. Whenever China has gotten good at offering cheap versions of strategic technologies like solar panels, electric vehicles, and drones, the US government has tried to stop it from flooding the market by using tariffs or rules on how government agencies purchase the tech. Such moves are always followed by debates about whether the trade-offs-particularly higher prices for consumers-are worth the benefits. But robotics is now best seen as another piece of the AI industry-in many ways its cutting edge. And the Trump administration is taking an increasingly aggressive approach to protecting the US AI industry, reportedly considering a ban on open-source Chinese models that often rival those from OpenAI and Anthropic while costing far less. Such a move would block businesses from realizing an estimated $25 billion in annual savings. The ban on humanoids, then, should be understood not as another chapter in the old China trade playbook, but as evidence that the Trump administration is expanding its protection of the AI industry beyond today's leading labs. It is now willing to step in on behalf of an emerging robotics sector that is still barely finding its footing. Some US robotics companies unsurprisingly welcome the FTC's new move. Gavin Kenneally, CEO of a company called Ghost Robotics that makes four-legged robots for inspections, says the cybersecurity risks from foreign-made robots are real (an FTC document released as part of the ruling cited an incident in which a man was able to gain control of 7,000 robot vacuum cleaners). "If today's announcement encourages stronger cybersecurity and a more level competitive environment, that's good for customers and good for the robotics industry," Kenneally said in an email. But if the new rule aims to boost US robotics companies, there's a big flaw. Those companies, as well as academic robotics labs, are hugely reliant on cheap robots from China to do research. They're building fleets of robots that constantly learn new tasks-from flipping waffles to doing laundry-and frequently buy Chinese humanoids instead of US-made ones. The new ruling "creates a challenge for US humanoid researchers," says Aaron Prather, director of market intelligence for the Association for Advancing Automation, a robotics trade group. "Chinese models offer the best price-to-capability ratio available." Prather adds that a recent internal review his organization conducted found that 90% of recent robotics research papers from US universities relied on robots from Unitree, China's top humanoid robotics company. That price gap can be huge. A four-legged robot from Unitree can cost around $4,600. A comparable one from Boston Dynamics might run to $278,000. If robotics research is stunted because these cheap robots are no longer available, the FTC ruling could slow down the industry, not boost it. The US and Chinese robotics industries are in starkly different places. Unitree plans to go public this week, targeting a nearly $6 billion evaluation. No robotics companies in the US offer any meaningful comparison, but those that do exist are undeniably moving fewer robots. Figure's humanoids are not yet selling at scale, and 1X's robots aren't yet shipping to homes. That said, work on humanoids is going increasingly mainstream, as a release from Google last week made clear. The company announced a new AI model meant to make humanoids learn new tasks faster; its most impressive ability appears to be tying a trash bag, but given how finicky robot hands are, that's real progress. Even though the many carve-outs in the FTC's order make its practical impact hard to predict, its symbolic impact is easy to see. The administration sees humanoid robotics not as a novelty, but as a strategic frontier of AI worth protecting from foreign competition. For a technology that until recently was mostly known for falling over onstage, that's a big change.

title: The first-gen Kindle Scribe is a big e-reader and digital notebook that’s $150 refurbished

summary: This article compares two leading digital note-takers, the Kindle Scribe and the Remarkable Paper Pro. Both are marketed to students for academic use. While both devices are discounted through Woot, users should note differences in warranty coverage and specific hardware capabilities.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: The Kindle Scribe is worth considering if you're heading back to school, as its large 10.2-inch screen can display textbooks and ebooks, or let you jot down handwritten notes during class. Now through August 8th, the first-gen model (with a Premium Pen) is down to just $149.99 with 16GB of storage in refurbished condition at Woot when you apply the promo code KINDLE25 at checkout. That's $220 off its original launch price from 2022 and even cheaper than the current Kindle Paperwhite , though you'll only get Woot's 90-day warranty. Woot doesn't specify the exact condition of its refurbished devices, but it does offer a brief explanation here of what to expect. The Kindle Scribe features a sharp 300ppi E Ink display that's glare-free and supports adjustable color temperatures, making it easy to read whether you're outside in the sun or studying late at night. Like all other Kindles, the Scribe gives you quick and easy access to Amazon's massive store of digital books, so you can switch between assigned reading and your favorite novels without carrying multiple books or devices. It's not waterproof like the Kindle Paperwhite, though, so you'll want to keep it away from the pool and be careful when it rains. It's also a solid digital notebook, with the device offering a variety of pre-made templates for everything from lined paper and planners to to-do lists. After updating the software, the original Kindle Scribe also includes the same AI-powered note-taking features as the newer models, allowing you to jot down notes directly on compatible ebook pages, summarize and refine your handwritten notes, generate AI-powered summaries, and more.

title: Europe’s AI labeling and transparency rules are now in effect
teaser: 🚨 New EU rules mandate labeling all AI deepfakes and synthetic content—companies face fines up to 3% of global turnover.
summary:
The EU has implemented stringent transparency rules under the landmark AI Act, aiming to combat misinformation by making it mandatory for companies to label synthetic content and interactions. Effective August 2nd, 'providers' must notify users when interacting with an AI model and embed machine-readable marks on all generated content (text, audio, video, images). Simultaneously, 'deployers' must clearly label deepfakes and manipulated media.
These rules require tech platforms to ensure consumers can distinguish authentic human content from artificial creations. Non-compliance carries severe penalties: fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover. Although models launched before August 2nd have a grace period until December 2nd, the immediate enforcement signals major regulatory oversight in generative AI.
author: Jess Weatherbed
content: The European Union has ushered in some additional rules that aim to make it easier for people to identify chatbots and AI deepfakes online. The new transparency obligations under the bloc's landmark AI Act came into effect on August 2nd , requiring companies to disclose when people are interacting with AI models, and if content has been generated or altered by them. The transparency rules differ between providers (companies that develop and market AI systems) and deployers (platforms and services that use those AI systems), though some companies like Meta and SpaceXAI are classified as both. Providers must design AI systems to explicitly notify users when they're dealing with AI instead of a human, "unless this is obvious," and include machine-readable marks on synthetic audio, image, video, and text so that it can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated. Likewise, deployers are required to label any AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, and video deepfake content that's designed to look real. "The rapid development of generative and interactive AI systems is making it increasingly difficult to distinguish AI interactions and AI-generated content from human-created and authentic content," the European Commission said in its transparency guidelines . "People should know when they are interacting with AI or exposed to AI-generated content. This will help them make informed decisions, calibrate their trust and reliance on AI and avoid misinformation or deception." The Commission has also developed a set of AI disclosure labels that tech platforms can adopt in accordance with the AI Act rules, alongside examples of when they should be used. These mirror similar labels that have already been introduced by TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook. The EU-made icons have been introduced to prevent platforms from having to design their own, and while the EU examples are optional to use, the Commission pointedly notes that its labeling requirements "are not." Companies that fail to comply with these new transparency rules risk facing fines of up to €15 million (about $17.2 million), or 3 percent of their global annual turnover. While the new transparency rules are enforceable immediately for new AI systems, any models and services that launched before August 2nd have a four-month grace period until December 2nd to comply.

title: WhatsApp says it is is fixing an issue that disabled several accounts
teaser: WhatsApp reported a widespread issue where millions of accounts were suddenly blocked or put 'under review' by Meta.
summary: Multiple WhatsApp users reported sudden difficulties accessing their accounts, which were placed 'under review' by Meta. The platform displayed a notice stating that account activity and device information were being checked against Terms of Service. Meta confirmed the outage, acknowledging they are working to restore access to affected accounts for its network of over 3 billion monthly active users. While the company noted these actions help curb abuse, it conceded that mistakes happen and efforts are underway to fix the problem quickly.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: For the last few hours, several people across social media have reported that their WhatsApp accounts have been blocked and put "under review" by Meta. The company, in response to TechCrunch's inquiries about the matter, said that it is working on restoring access to these accounts. According to posts from those impacted on X and Threads , many were suddenly unable to use their accounts. When they tried to access their accounts, WhatsApp displayed a screen that said, "Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our Terms of Service. We'll notify you of the result typically within 24 hours." Meta's popular chat app has more than 3 billion monthly active users across the world, making even a proportionally small disruption one that can impact thousands of users. Meta acknowledged the issue and told TechCrunch the company is working on resolving it. However, it didn't specify if users in specific regions were impacted, or what caused the problem. "We are always working to stay ahead of those trying to abuse our service and ban accounts to help keep other users safe. Sometimes we get this wrong, and if we do, we try to fix it as quickly as possible to get people back to chatting. We've taken action to restore affected accounts," a company spokesperson said. The company didn't provide details around what caused a bunch of accounts to go under review.
