title: Apple challenges UK government’s latest demand for iCloud backdoor: report
teaser: Apple is challenging the UK government’s demand for an iCloud backdoor into users' end-to-end encrypted data, citing privacy rights.
summary: Apple is legally challenging repeated demands from the U.K. government to access its users' encrypted iCloud data. The core issue revolves around the 'technical capability notice,' a secret legal order demanding access even when data is protected by Advanced Data Protection (ADP). ADP secures backups with end-to-end encryption, meaning only the customer can access it, including Apple itself. Critics argue that such demands effectively require a government 'backdoor.' This current dispute follows a previous highly publicized conflict between Apple and the U.K. over encrypted backups.
author: Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai
content: Apple is challenging another legal demand by the U.K. government to access the encrypted data of its users in the country, according to Financial Times . The company reportedly filed a complaint with the U.K.'s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, a court that hears cases related to government surveillance, after the government last year issued a "technical capability notice." The notice is a secret government legal order for demanding access to users' data, even if the data is encrypted. For critics, this kind of demand is the equivalent of requesting a backdoor into Apple's cloud backups that have Advanced Data Protection (ADP) switched on, which makes the data end-to-end encrypted and inaccessible to anyone other than the customer, including Apple. This new challenge comes a year after a similar fight between Apple and the U.K. government. In early 2025, London issued a secret order to Apple demanding access to users' encrypted iCloud backups, which was later dropped following the intervention of the Trump administration. After the first order, the company reacted by removing the ability of U.K. users to use ADP. Then, in October, the U.K. issued a second order , which Apple is now challenging. Apple did not respond to TechCrunch's request for comment.

title: AWS is helping vibe-coding startup Superblocks, and the implications are big
teaser: Superblocks partners with AWS, allowing its tools to run entirely within private enterprise clouds—meaning business data never leaves the premises.
summary: Vibe-coding startup Superblocks has partnered with AWS to embed its tools directly into the private clouds of enterprise customers. This ensures that sensitive business data never leaves the company's secure network, using services like Amazon Aurora databases and integrating with Amazon Bedrock for AI capabilities. While this move aligns with a broader trend where cloud providers urge businesses to keep their entire AI stack internally, industry experts note that CIOs are already pushing back by favoring multi-model strategies to prevent vendor lock-in, making the security implications of these partnerships highly significant.
author: Julie Bort
content: Vibe-coding startup Superblocks announced a multiyear joint marketing agreement with Amazon Web Services (AWS) that enables its tool to be embedded within the private clouds of AWS customers. That means an enterprise on AWS that subscribes to Superblocks will be able to offer vibe coding to the company's business users, and those apps will not send data or information externally to model providers or databases. The apps will spin up Amazon Aurora databases within the company's private cloud, not, for instance, create external Supabase databases, the vibe-coding database of choice . The apps will also integrate with Amazon Bedrock , the cloud giant's AI app development/AI gateway/inference platform. Essentially, these apps will automatically fall under IT's management and security, rather than be rogue applications. "We're going to bring it to your data inside your private cloud," Superblocks co-founder and CEO Brad Menezes tells TechCrunch of vibe coding. "The big thing about that is data never leaves. ... It's their AWS account and basically secure with all of the auditing, all of the encryption, all of the network controls." AWS will also help sell Superblocks to enterprises as it does for many of its Marketplace partners. "We support partners where we see strong customer demand and alignment with how customers want to build," an AWS spokesperson tells TechCrunch. Still, AWS does not yet have its own vibe-coding agent aimed at business users. It has Kiro, an AI coding agent aimed at developers. Amazon also has an AI assistant, Quick, for business users. But again, that's more like a Claude Cowork or Microsoft Copilot, rather than a Lovable or Replit. So this should be a nice boost for early-stage Superblocks, which has 50 employees and raised a total of $60 million as of its Series A , announced in May 2025, backed by Spark Capital, Kleiner Perkins, Meritech Capital, and Greenoaks. Yet, it's actually a more significant symbol than that. It's part of a growing trend where the hyperscaler cloud providers urge their enterprise customers to separate their AI models from all the other scaffolding needed to run enterprise AI and do so on their clouds. They want enterprises to buy AI harnesses (aka agentic apps), AI orchestration, security tools, and the like from them, and not from the frontier providers. In the past few weeks, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been banging the drum with exactly that message. He's been telling his many enterprise customers to use multiple models to reduce costs and avoid lock-in . He's also been preaching that the AI labs are not trustworthy enough to turn to for agent orchestration or app-level harnesses because they may use that data to study a business and later compete with it. Enterprises perhaps don't need such warnings. They have already decided to adopt multiple models, particularly frontier Chinese open-weight options. "That is flipped because 60 days ago they were like, I want a specific model. It's called Anthropic," Menezes adds. Open models, for instance, accounted for 29% of all traffic routed through Vercel's AI gateway last month, a popular tool among enterprises to manage multi-model AI use. Then, by necessity, all of their AI scaffolding can't be tied to one provider. "Having a multi-model strategy across big frontier labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, and open source - and I'd say Chinese open source right now, but also U.S. open source is now starting to come up. It's a must-have for the CIO," he says. They want model choice for coding as well as customer service, HR, [and] sales automation, he adds. Menezes says the movement is so strong, he predicts that "any enterprise that is betting on a single model provider, that executive will be fired." So now we're seeing the cloud providers bring vibe coding for business users into private, secure clouds, too. That's like a potential second wave after bringing AI coding agents for enterprise developers. "It's an emerging category with real momentum, and exactly the kind of innovation we support," AWS tells TechCrunch.

title: Your Fitbit data can now connect directly to Apple Health
teaser: Fitbit data finally connects directly to Apple Health via Google's new 5.05 update, eliminating years of workarounds for fitness enthusiasts.
summary: Google has rolled out an update allowing Fitbit users to directly connect their fitness and vital data (workouts, steps, etc.) to Apple Health. This major feature eliminates the need for third-party workarounds that were previously required, as Google Health's 5.05 update now permits two-way syncing. Additionally, the update allows US users to use Smart Health Links—a function where individuals can generate a URL or QR code to securely share selected medical records with doctors or family members.
author: Emma Roth
content: Google is rolling out an update that will finally allow you to connect your Fitbit workouts, steps, vitals, and other data to Apple Health, as reported earlier by 9to5Mac . With Google Health's 5.05 update , you can now tap your profile icon, select "Partner apps," and choose Apple Health to link your data directly. Previously, you could only import your Apple Health data into Google Health, but not the other way around. That meant using third-party apps - like Power Sync for Fitbit or Fitbit to Apple Health Sync - or some other kind of workaround to connect your Google Health information to Apple Health. Google Health replaced the Fitbit app in May. The new app had a bit of a rocky rollout after users raised concerns over the new AI health coach, user interface, and other issues, though Google has since addressed some of these complaints. Along with this update, Google announced that users in the US can use Smart Health Links to share medical records with a provider or family member. You can create a link by heading to the Health tab, choosing the "Medical" section, selecting "Shareable records," and tapping the "plus" icon. From there, you can choose which data you want to include in the link and share it via a URL or QR code.

title: Snap CEO sidesteps Specs preorder questions on Q2 earnings call
teaser: Despite the $2,195 price tag, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel is banking on its 'first mover' status to conquer smart glasses market rivals like Apple and Meta.
summary:
During his recent earnings call, Snap CEO Evan Spiegel deflected investor questions about preorder demand for Specs, the company’s new smart glasses priced at $2,195. Instead of addressing immediate sales numbers, Spiegel emphasized that consumers need a hands-on experience to appreciate the technical advancements. He defended Snap's strategy against giants like Apple and Meta by highlighting its 'first mover' advantage in developing a new computing platform.

While acknowledging that weight and cost must decrease for mass adoption (expected later in the decade), he expressed confidence in the long-term opportunity. Spiegel stressed that achieving this product is technically complex, allowing Snap to leverage its early position to build out the ecosystem.
author: Aisha Malik
content: Snap CEO Evan Spiegel sidestepped investors' questions about preorder demand for the company's long-awaited Specs smart glasses during Monday's earnings call, just weeks before the device's September launch event. "What we're hearing from folks is really that they want to try Specs," Spiegel told investors. "It's obviously a high consideration purchase at $2,195. Obviously, developers and folks who are familiar with the platform really understand it and understand the technical leaps we've made with this generation. I think for the broader public and consumers, it's going to be really important for folks to go hands-on. Our upcoming launch event will be an important sort of starting point for that consumer-oriented journey." The company unveiled Specs in June after spending more than a decade developing the device. The wearable's $2,195 price tag is significantly higher than most Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, which start at around $350, but lower than Apple's Vision Pro, which starts at $3,500. Investors also pressed Spiegel on why he believes Snap's strategy is financially viable for a company of its size, why it chose to go it alone rather than partner with another company, and what gives him confidence that the company can compete with Apple, Meta, and Alphabet. Spiegel responded that Snap believes the long-term opportunity to develop the next computing platform is "enormous." "I think what some folks maybe don't understand yet, especially because Specs are so new and we're really the first mover in this category, is how difficult the product is to execute from a technical perspective," Spiegel said. "When we started innovating in the social space, we were a late entrant. So, most of the apps at the time, whether it was Facebook or Instagram or Twitter, were already in existence, and we had to really innovate to continue to grow. What's so unique about this opportunity for us is really that we're a first mover, and that really plays to our strengths as an innovator." When asked about product-market fit, Spiegel said it will likely be closer to the end of the decade before the company sees mass-market consumer adoption. "I think things, for example, like weight and cost are going to have to come down to see you know unit volumes really meaningfully pick up." But we do have, I think, a real advantage here in that developers have been building on the Specs platform now for several years."

title: Big Walk is like co-op Breath of the Wild
teaser: Big Walk offers a unique co-op puzzle experience, letting players share the discovery joy that made games like Breath of the Wild so special.
summary: Big Walk is a co-op multiplayer puzzle game from House House that tasks players with exploring a large island together. Unlike predecessor titles, it emphasizes collaborative discovery; progress relies heavily on communicating via proximity chat to solve puzzles, which can be tailored for 2-4 players (supporting up to 12). Players guide non-species spheres across the unmapped island searching for 'nubbins.' While some time spent hiking might feel tedious, the deep collaborative moments and sense of unexpected discovery are praised, drawing comparisons to The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. The game launches on August 4th for Nintendo Switch 2, PS5, and Steam.
author: Jay Peters
content: Untitled Goose Game is a tough act to follow. It was a silly experience that captured what I imagine it would feel like to be a sentient goose: a lot of waddling, a lot of honking, and a lot of shenanigans. That's why Big Walk , the next game from Goose Game developer House House, feels like a radical and unexpected departure . Instead of playing as a goose terrorizing a small village, Big Walk is a co-op multiplayer game where you explore a large island and have to work together to solve puzzles. I've been playing Big Walk as a duo with my wife, and while we're not done yet, we've spent more than 13 hours exploring the island and solving problems together. Big Walk may be a comparatively small game, but the experience of making unexpected discoveries can make it feel like a grand adventure in the Zelda mold. The name Big Walk suggests a game about walking - and there is indeed much walking - but it's really more about talking. Outside of some brief signage about the controls, the game doesn't give you explicit guidance about how to play, where to go, or what puzzles to tackle. Instead, you have to rely on communicating with your fellow players over proximity chat (or a neat proximity text system) to figure things out. Puzzles can scale to fit two to four players, but as many as 12 people can inhabit a game at the same time. Solving puzzles can be a tall task. Image: Panic You play as sentient spheres with arms and legs that don't look like any species I've ever seen, tasked with collecting curious red balls we've been calling "nubbins." You'll need to stay in touch to navigate the island, which is filled with bushes, sloping hills, and odd buildings that make it easy to get lost. When the sun sets, things get really dark, which forces you to use lanterns and stick together. Big Walk also doesn't give you a map menu or golden arrows telling you where to go, so it's up to you and your friends to figure out how to traverse the island. Big Walk is crafted so that something interesting is usually hidden just around the corner, like a new landmark, a tool of some kind, and even tall towers. More often than not, you'll stumble across some kind of brightly colored building that features a puzzle you have to work together to solve, like chatting from opposite sides of a wall to figure out how to put some tiles in the correct order. Sometimes, Big Walk even separates players so that you can't use proximity chat at all. Coming up with ways to communicate is difficult given that your character can basically only point, jump, and hold things. That means the moments when my wife and I have been separated to solve a puzzle have genuinely been nail-biters. My heart was actually racing when I kicked a ticking kitchen timer up a hill and hoped that I had given my wife enough time to drop it in the right spot. Often, when you have to figure out some sort of code to solve a puzzle, the game forces you to wait for a few agonizing seconds to know if you completed it correctly. When you do get one done, you'll see a joyful burst of confetti and get a new nubbin. Even the breaks are fun. Image: Panic The way Big Walk is structured has some pitfalls. You'll spend a lot of time just hiking around the island to get somewhere new, which can be tedious. You can't do much in the game without at least one other person, so that means you have to match up when you want to play with whoever else is in your group. At the end of a long day, sometimes my wife and I didn't want to hop into the game to walk slowly, get lost, and solve hard puzzles. Our conversations were often punctuated by yawns, which any fellow parents with a toddler will understand. But Big Walk 's constraints are also what make it so remarkable. While hiking around and promising ourselves we'd seek out a single puzzle for the evening, we'd often decompress about our day and catch up on things. When we found a puzzle, we'd get extremely invested in figuring it out. After we solved it, we'd usually have the energy to tackle another one. We even figured out how to use the limited moveset to give each other high-fives and hugs. Many of the elements that made Goose Game great are present in Big Walk . There's a lot of walking, a lot of talking, and a lot of shenanigans. While playing Big Walk , however, I also kept thinking of a very different game. The sense of discovery and joy are much like what made The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild so special, whether that was finding a kooky way to solve a puzzle, stumbling upon an extremely useful item, or climbing to the highest peak and taking in the view. But unlike Breath of the Wild , Big Walk let me share the world, and those moments of discovery, with my best friend. Big Walk launches August 4th on the Nintendo Switch 2, PS5, and Steam. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Jay Peters Entertainment Games Review Gaming

title: Lenovo Googlebook leaks reveal a laptop and 2-in-1 tablet
teaser: Googlebook successors ditch ChromeOS for AI-powered systems; leaks show Lenovo laptops/tablets featuring new Gemini keys.
summary: Google has announced its next-generation Chromebook successor, branded as Googlebook. Leaked images from Lenovo reveal both a laptop and a 2-in-1 tablet planned for release in Fall 2026 across multiple brands (including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo). Crucially, the devices are expected to abandon ChromeOS for an entirely new operating system heavily integrated with Gemini AI. The leaked models feature updated hardware: the laptop has a back light strip, and both units include a dedicated 'G' key designed specifically to launch Gemini AI.
author: Jess Weatherbed
content: Lenovo is expected to release some of the first Googlebook models later this year, and leaked images have now given us a good idea of what they might look like. Leaked press images shared by Digital Citizen and Android Headlines include a laptop and a 2-in-1 tablet, all of which feature Googlebook branding on the keyboard. This is the best look we've had at Google's Chromebook successor since the Android-based Googlebook platform was announced in May . Details about the initiative remain sparse, but we know that Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo are lined up to release the first models sometime in Fall 2026. Googlebooks are also expected to ditch ChromeOS in favor of a new operating system, and Gemini AI will reportedly be baked into pretty much everything. The Lenovo leaks look fairly similar to Lenovo's existing Chromebook lineup, with a few exceptions. The Lenovo Googlebook laptop appears to be available in two sizes, and features a light strip on the back that resembles the glowing bar that appears on the official Googlebook renders that Google released earlier this year. The 2-in-1 tablet also includes a light bar on the rear camera housing - similar to the glowing orb that will reportedly feature on the upcoming Pixel 11 lineup . The keyboards also include a new key on the bottom row that displays Google's "G" branding. Digital Citizen reports that this is a dedicated hardware key to surface Gemini, but it's worth noting that the keyboards also include a Quick Insert button where the cap lock key is - something that Chromebooks introduced to call up Gemini back in 2024.

title: Samsung’s 2TB 9100 Pro SSD is actually somewhat reasonably priced
teaser: Samsung’s high-speed 9100 Pro SSD is currently priced lower on Amazon, offering PCIe Gen 5 performance for tech enthusiasts.
summary: Samsung's 2TB 9100 Pro SSD offers high performance at a favorable price point, currently available on Amazon for $302.99. This model is significant as it is Samsung’s first to support the ultra-fast PCIe Gen 5 standard, boasting read and write speeds at least double those of its predecessor, the 990 Pro. While ideal for systems equipped with the necessary motherboard infrastructure, the 9100 Pro also performs well in a PCIe Gen 4 setup without requiring a heatsink in a PC or laptop. However, users should note that installing a heatsink is mandatory if using the SSD in a PlayStation 5 to prevent potential damage from overheating.
author: Cameron Faulkner
content: Next to buying RAM, finding a fast, high-capacity NVMe SSD at a reasonable price has been a challenge during RAMageddon. I don't want to say it's getting easier, but one of Samsung's latest SSDs is cheaper than it has sold for since February 2026. That's something, right? Amazon has the heatsink-less version of the Samsung 9100 Pro with 2TB of storage for $302.99, which is about $100 less than the usual price. Granted, it sold for a low of $169.99 back in October 2025, but it's a smart purchase right now compared to buying the 1TB model for $250. The 9100 Pro is Samsung's first SSD to support PCIe Gen 5, making it a great fit if you have the right motherboard and other parts to get as much speed from it as possible. Its theoretical maximum random read and write speeds are at least twice as fast as the 990 Pro SSD that it replaced. However, it's good (albeit slower than advertised) in a PCIe Gen 4 setup, as well. It'll work fine without a heatsink in a PC or laptop (though, it's never a bad idea to use one that fits in your system). However, you'll need to install a heatsink in order to use this in a PlayStation 5, due to potential heat issues that could damage the SSD if used without one. Thankfully, heatsinks are super affordable , and come in a range of designs and price points.

title: Congress’s favorite AI tool? ChatGPT
teaser: ChatGPT dominates congressional AI spending, receiving 90% of all documented funds from House offices for legislative tasks.
summary: According to a CNBC report citing House disbursement records, OpenAI's ChatGPT is Congress’s most widely used AI tool by expenditure. During the year ending March 31, Congress spent $100,580 on ChatGPT alone, accounting for roughly 90% of total documented spending across various offices and committees. Anthropic's Claude followed in second place with $13,160. The data also revealed a significant partisan split: Democratic offices spent $54,165, three times more than the $15,782 spent by Republican offices. Staffers are adopting these paid AI tools for core legislative functions, including analyzing and summarizing legislation, preparing hearing materials, writing memos, responding to constituents, and drafting policy research.
author: Rebecca Bellan
content: OpenAI's ChatGPT is Congress's AI tool of choice so far in terms of money spent, according to a report from CNBC . OpenAI received roughly 90% of all spending on AI tools by House offices, committees and institutional accounts during the year ending in March 31, per House disbursement records. CNBC found that Congress spent around $100,580 across 798 transactions on ChatGPT, out of at least $113,740 in total AI spending. Anthropic's Claude trailed in second place at $13,160 across 37 transactions. Democratic offices accounted for $54,165 in AI purchases, three times the $15,782 spent by Republican offices. The insights exclude any Congressional AI adoption from free accounts or AI bundled into broader software contracts. Congressional staffers are using ChatGPT and other tools to write memos, summarize and analyze legislation, respond to constituents, prepare hearing materials, sort through policy research, and even draft social media posts.

title: Outernet turns your saved posts into real-world adventures
teaser: Outernet turns social media likes into tangible adventures: Save online posts to generate real-life scavenger hunts in your city.
summary: Outernet is an innovative startup designed to bridge the gap between online inspiration and real-world action. The app allows users to save sightings—such as local events or restaurants—from platforms like Instagram by sharing posts directly into Outernet. Utilizing AI, it automatically extracts critical details like dates, times, and locations, organizing them into a functional itinerary. The founders emphasize that their unique strength lies in community organizing, making the app's mission: to be the 'motivation engine for IRL.' Beyond tracking, the app plans a gamified 'passport book' feature. Having already accumulated 18,000 users and generating revenue through premium subscriptions ($6.99/mo), Outernet is actively expanding its reach.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Danielle Egan and Athena Leong know how to have fun. Between the two of them, they've organized a citywide scavenger hunt in San Francisco and turned a viral prank into an exclusive NYC restaurant for a night. They even created an alternative to a running club for socializing, dubbed a "sit club ," where people just bring their chairs and relax. Now, with their new startup, Outernet , the co-founders want to help others add more fun to their lives, too. The app's name is inspired by the concept of using the internet as a tool to get you to go outside, hence "outernet." It's one of several apps that helps you save the things you see online - like local events, restaurants or bars to try, or other city landmarks - and turn them into a list of to-dos for exploring the world around you. Outernet's pitch is that instead of simply liking a post about something you'd like to see or do on social media, you should share it to its app, where it will track the activity or place you want to visit for you in an organized interface. (Invite codes to try the app for yourself are at the bottom of this post). What makes Outernet different from others in the space, like Albo, Tabi, or Plotline, is who's behind it: founders who have devoted much of their time to playfulness and having fun offline. Now, they want to bring that same spirit into their app. Image Credits: Outernet "In my free time, I'm very passionate about getting people to go outside and do things," explains Egan , whose offline persona is quite different from her former day job working in product BizOps at LinkedIn. "I just love capturing attention in unexpected ways and delivering delightful things." She says the thesis behind the app is becoming the "motivation engine for IRL" - something that removes the friction between wanting to do something and actually going out to do it. Outernet taps into an already common consumer behavior. As you scroll TikTok and Instagram, you're often inspired by a creator's post, so you'll save it in the app as a reminder. But then you promptly forget about the idea as you continue to consume more content. Outernet solves this problem by keeping track of the things you want to do or places you want to visit, all in one place. Image Credits: Outernet To save a post to the app, you'll tap the share option from the source app, like TikTok or Instagram, then scroll through the list of places you can share to until you find Outernet. You can also paste in social media URLs or website links directly into the app, or upload a photo of something you see, like a flyer. To organize everything, Outernet leverages AI to pull relevant information, like the date, time, location, and details about the activity you want to try or the location of a place you'd like to visit. Events are saved to a chronological feed, which you can revisit whenever you're looking for something to do. Other activities without a date, as well as places you'd like to visit, are organized into separate tabs within the app. You can also save events to your Apple or Google Calendar or view them in Outernet's map. Image Credits: Outernet The app can also send proactive reminders and nudges that encourage you to go do the things you've saved. Then, as you explore places in the real world, you can "stamp" them as such, building what will eventually become a passport documenting your activities. Image Credits: Outernet "We're thinking of different ways of creating maybe some sort of like passport book where you can look at all the things [you've done] and maybe share that with friends and get some sort of sense of pride of that," Egan says of future product plans. They're also thinking of using traditional gamification techniques to encourage activity, like giving out stamps when you reach different milestones. The idea for Outernet came out of the co-founders' experience designing a citywide scavenger hunt in San Francisco, called "Pursuit," which began three years ago and is now held annually. The monthlong game drew participation from about 1.5% of San Francisco's population during its most recent run. As the founders chatted with participants, they found that people didn't get involved because they loved scavenger hunts or adventure games; they just wanted an excuse to go outside. This sparked an idea. "We just realized that people really have an appetite for doing things, like going on adventures. This is the new trend," notes Leong , whose background is in computer science and child development, before she landed a job in adventure game design. "There are so many incredible community events, and being community organizers ourselves, we're very plugged into that scene," Egan adds. "What's so hard is there are these boots on the ground - incredible community organizers who are hosting these amazing events, and they just don't know how to reach people because marketing and grabbing people's attention is such a different skill set. And that's something that we are exceptional in. So we see ourselves as the conduit," she says. Outernet's app has been on the market for roughly two months and is already profitable from its premium subscription ($6.99/mo or $39.99/year), which lets you save more items per day. It has around 18,000 users in total, and the team is experimenting rapidly with new ideas. The founders are now having casual conversations with investors about their next steps, but finding the right fit is key. "We want to bring on investors - if we do - [who are] people who are really aligned with us," says Leong. "We're whimsical, and we have to find investors that match." Outernet is invite-only and available on iOS , with an Android waitlist . TechCrunch readers can use the invite code "coffeewalk" to skip the waitlist.

title: Samsung’s discounted smart monitor is $349.99, its lowest price yet
teaser: Samsung's versatile M80F monitor ($349.99) and the QD-OLED G50SF gaming panel (as low as $300) are available at steeply discounted prices.
summary: Samsung is making high-quality monitors more accessible through deep discounts on two models: the M80F and the G50SF. The versatile M80F, a 32-inch 4K panel that combines computer monitor functions with television features (including streaming apps and a removable webcam), is discounted to $349.99. For dedicated gamers, the QD-OLED Samsung G50SF offers excellent specs—like an up to 180Hz refresh rate and .03-millisecond response time—and is currently available around $300. Both options provide significant value compared to their original or competitor pricing.
author: Brad Bourque
content: Samsung makes a variety of TVs and computer monitors, but if want both and you're limited on space, you might want to consider the M80F . This capable 32-inch 4K panel combines features commonly found on both types of screens, and Amazon and B&H Photo both have it discounted to $349.99, where it's usually $400 or much higher. In addition to acting as a standard 4K screen for your computer or console, the M80F has a full suite of video streaming apps you'd expect to find on a television, with picture-in-picture support for multitasking, plus a removable webcam for video chats. The M80F has above-average connectivity for a monitor. In addition to the ports like HDMI 2.0, USB-C for charging devices up to 65W, and USB-A for your keyboard and mouse, you can also connect the Tizen interface to Wi-Fi to directly communicate with your network (it also supports Bluetooth headphones). Speaking of gaming, the M80F supports apps like Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now, letting you pair a controller to the display to play games over the cloud. The VA panel is better suited for work than play, but HDR10 Plus support will help your movies and TV shows pop. My colleague Cameron Faulkner reviewed a previous version of the M80F and appreciated its versatility, but the $699.99 launch price was a bit off-putting, so a discount on a newer, improved model is definitely worth calling out.

title: IT boss left root session open for bring-your-kid-to-work day
teaser: A bring-your-kid tech day taught one IT boss a lesson: letting your daughter type 'SHUTDOWN' on an RS/6000 root session can cost 36 hours of repairs.
summary: In an amusing tech anecdote, a reader recounted how an IT boss set up his work environment for a bring-your-kid day using an IBM RS/6000 Unix machine. The boss left the system running and logged in as 'root,' providing access to terminals connected to the ancient Unix OS. When his nine-year-old daughter typed the command "SHUTDOWN," mimicking a movie, she inadvertently caused significant damage that required 36 hours to repair.
content: OS PLATFORMS IT boss left root session open for bring-your-kid-to-work day Daddy, I typed a Unix command! Was it a bad one? WHO, ME? Comedian W.C. Fields is credited with the aphorism "Never work with children or animals," which The Register mentions because half of it has some relevance to this week's edition of "Who, Me?" - the reader-contributed column chronicling the ups and downs of working in tech. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Stockley" who shared a horror story that took place in the 1990s. At the time, Stockley worked for a company that ran an IBM RS/6000, one of Big Blue's brood of Unix machines. "The business was run on BASIC, with code going back 25 years," Stockley wrote. When much of that software was written, memory was measured in kilobytes. "Programs had to be broken into chunks, which were called sequentially with the CHAIN command," he told Who, Me? The company's tech may have been a bit crusty, but it made up for that by being a lovely family-friendly workplace - so much so that it invited staff to bring their kids in for Halloween trick-or-treating. Stockley told us that one Halloween, the company's IT boss knew the children would disrupt work, so started the day's data processing early, setting the chained programs in motion. Then his wife and children arrived ahead of the Halloween festivities. The boss therefore parked his children in his office, in front of terminals connected to the RS/6000. The terminals were switched on and logged in as root. In Stockley's telling, the boss's nine-year-old daughter had recently seen a movie in which a young girl somehow acquired Unix skills and saved the day by typing "SHUTDOWN." And when the boss returned to his office, his daughter greeted him by saying: "Look, Daddy! SHUTDOWN worked just like it did in the movie!" Stockley recalls that the boss needed 36 hours to repair the damage his daughter had caused. Have kids messed with your tech? If so, don't mess about!
